# Conclusion

This study has investigated to what extent students' social networks are segregated on parental
education level and what the effect of having parents with the same educational level is on a
student's social satisfaction. The data used to investigate this question was from one of the
Michigan Learning Communities, consisting of 121 students. For analysis, Stochastic Action Oriented
Models were used. This study has posed four research questions:

1.  "To what extent is the MLC network segregated based on parental education level?"
2.  "To what extent do reciprocated friendships among students with parents with the same
    educational level occur?"
3.  "To what extent do reciprocated friendships affect students' social satisfaction throughout the
    year?"
4.  "To what extent do reciprocated friendships among students with parents with the same education
    level affect their social satisfaction throughout the year?"

The first question took a macro-perspective on the network. I used Moran's I and Coleman's homophily
index to answer this question and concluded that the first hypothesis "The MLC network is segregated
on parental education level" should be rejected as the statistics did not indicate that this was the
case. This is interesting, because it contrasts what other studies have found previously (see:
[@ZWIER2023127]). However, this study took place in an American context and additionally, other
studies have also taken into account the parental income-level. This finding indicates that
income-level might play a bigger role in SES-segregation.

The second question posed a micro-perspective and specifically looked into homophily among
reciprocated ties. The results seemed to indicate that students were rather less likely than more
likely to have reciprocated ties with other students whose parents had the same educational level,
though this was not significant. Therefore, the second hypothesis "Reciprocated ties are more likely
to exist among students with parents with the same educational level" was also rejected. For the
control variables gender and ethnicity, this was also not the case. As reciprocity itself was
positive and significant, this shows that if a tie is send, it is likely that it well be
reciprocated, no matter the characteristics of the other person.

The third question assessed the effect of the network on behaviour. The behaviour, in this case, was
social satisfaction. Results showed that the effect of reciprocated ties on social satisfaction was
close to zero, indicating that reciprocation in friendship has no influence on social satisfaction.
This leads to the third hypothesis, "Reciprocated ties positively affect students' social
satisfaction" also being rejected.

The last question assessed an interaction effect of reciprocated ties between students whose parents
have the same educational level. This effect was positive, but not significant and therefore also
rejected. Additionally, the Goodness-of-Fit of this model was worse than the Goodness-of-Fit of the
model of question three. This indicates that there are other network or interaction effects that
affect change in behaviour, that are more influential than these characteristics. In both models,
the influence of the quadratic shape effect remained the biggest, indicating that students whose
social satisfaction is below the mean are likely to move towards the mean.

This study also has several limitations. Firstly, this study has not distinctly looked at students
whose parents are higher educated versus students whose parents are not higher educated, meaning
that the study has looked into, *overall*, does homophily in reciprocated ties affect social
satisfaction. It could be the case that this homophily does not have an influence on students whose
parents are higher educated and that their social satisfaction depends on other things, but that it
does have an influence on students whose parents are not higher educated. The study by [@melian2026]
suggests that this is indeed the case. The Michigan Learning Communities prioritises first
generation students and shape the program towards their needs [@rambaran2025], which could have
affected their social satisfaction. However, because I was limited to only one learning community,
the amount of students whose parents had not enjoyed higher education was relatively small, which
would have made it harder to assess the effect of homophily of reciprocated ties on their
friendships. This is why I have chosen to assess the overall effect of same parental education level
homophily on social satisfaction. Therefore, a future study could look into the effects specifically
for students whose parents have not enjoyed higher education. Additionally, the study could then
assess multiple learning communities, so network differences can be assessed.

Secondly, the Goodness-of-Fit models for the Outdegree Distribution and for the TriadCensus
distribution did not reach values that are desirable. This indicates that perhaps more or other
effects should have been included in the models to create a better fit. Additionally, the
Goodness-of-Fit of the Behavioural distribution worsened and overestimated the amount of people with
very high social satisfaction, indicating that here as well, other effects might were more relevant
for explaining changes in behaviour than the effects that were used in this study.

Another limitation of the study is that students that the indegree ties of students that were
missing in one of the two waves, were coded as a non-nomination in these waves. This could have led
to biases in certain statistics, such as transitivity, and reciprocity, which was my effect of
interest. When looking at the network graph provided in the descriptives, it can be seen that some
of the students who were big tie-senders and receivers in wave 1, were missing in wave 2. Would
their incoming ties have been included, it perhaps would have lead to different results.

While this study has not yielded significant results and knows its limitations, this does not mean
that the social network perspective is not relevant. Firstly, a social network perspective allowed
me to assess whether segregation takes place in a network and account for this. Would this study be
conducted over multiple communities and for a longer period of time, for example segregation helps
us to assess differences in a network and control for this. Perhaps a more segregated network also
has a different culture and different effects on students who do or do not befriend other students
whose parents have enjoyed a similar education level.

Additionally, a social network perspective gives the opportunity to assess different types of
networks, for example, the amount of ties ones has, how many triads it consists of and how many ties
are reciprocated. [@Wittner2023] has shown that for first generation students, it matters if their
network is for example close-knit or "have-it-all", as this influences how they manage at
universities. A social network perspective would enable one to take differences in these networks
into account in their analysis.

Lastly, this study has taken some control-variables into account, such as the average social
satisfaction of ones friends, as this can also influence ones social satisfaction. A linear
regression analysis, for example, would have not been able to do this, while friends can be of
important influential factors on how someone is feeling.
